content: 1. Monitor patients closely when co-administering digoxin with velpatasvir, as velpatasvir inhibits P-glycoprotein (P-gp). Regularly assess digoxin levels and adjust the dose if necessary, especially if digoxin concentrations increase by less than 50%. Refer to the prescribing information for digoxin for specific monitoring and dose adjustment recommendations. 2. Sotalol can increase the effects of digoxin through pharmacodynamic synergy. Use caution and monitor closely, as both drugs can elevate serum potassium levels. The combination of digoxin and sotalol may increase the risk of toxicity for either drug. Avoid or consider alternative therapies, as this combination can also increase the risk of bradycardia. 3. Sotagliflozin, when administered at 400 mg, can increase digoxin exposure through an unspecified interaction mechanism. Monitor digoxin levels closely and modify therapy as needed. 4. Spironolactone can increase digoxin levels by reducing renal clearance. Use caution and monitor closely, as both drugs can elevate serum potassium levels. Adjust therapy as necessary to avoid potential complications. 5. St. John’s Wort decreases digoxin levels by inducing P-glycoprotein (P-gp) efflux transporters and increasing metabolism. Use caution and monitor digoxin levels closely when co-administering these agents. 6. Stiripentol increases digoxin levels by inhibiting P-glycoprotein (P-gp) efflux transporters. Consider reducing the dose of P-gp substrates if adverse reactions occur during concomitant administration. Monitor closely. 7. Sucralfate decreases digoxin levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Avoid or use an alternative drug. Measure serum digoxin concentrations before initiating concomitant therapy and adjust the digoxin dose by approximately 20–40% if necessary. 8. Sulfamethoxazole and sulfadiazine increase digoxin levels by altering intestinal flora. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Use caution and monitor closely. 9. Sulfasalazine decreases digoxin levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. Both drugs can increase serum potassium levels. Use caution and monitor closely. 10. Suvorexant increases digoxin levels by inhibiting P-glycoprotein (P-gp) efflux transporters. Monitor digoxin levels closely, as this interaction may cause a slight increase in digoxin levels. 11. Tacrolimus increases digoxin levels by inhibiting P-glycoprotein (P-gp) efflux transporters. Use caution and monitor closely. 12. Teduglutide may increase digoxin levels by enhancing the absorption of concomitant oral medications. Use caution with drugs requiring titration or those with a narrow therapeutic index, as dose adjustments may be necessary. 13. Teicoplanin increases digoxin levels by altering intestinal flora. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Use caution and monitor closely. 14. Telmisartan increases digoxin levels through an unknown mechanism. Both drugs can elevate serum potassium levels. Use caution and monitor closely. 15. Tenofovir DF increases digoxin levels by reducing renal clearance. Use caution and monitor closely, as there is a potential for increased toxicity. 16. Tepotinib increases digoxin levels by inhibiting P-glycoprotein (P-gp) efflux transporters. Avoid or use an alternative drug. If concomitant use is unavoidable, reduce the P-gp substrate dosage as recommended in the product labeling. 17. Teriparatide increases digoxin toxicity due to transient hypercalcemia, which may predispose patients to digoxin toxicity. Use caution and monitor closely. 18. Tetracycline increases digoxin levels by altering intestinal flora. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Use caution and monitor closely. 19. Ticagrelor increases digoxin levels by inhibiting P-glycoprotein (P-gp) efflux transporters. Monitor digoxin levels closely when initiating or changing ticagrelor therapy. 20. Tigecycline increases digoxin levels by altering intestinal flora. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Monitor closely. 21. Timolol increases the effects of digoxin through pharmacodynamic synergy. Both drugs can elevate serum potassium levels. Avoid or use an alternative drug, as this combination can increase the risk of bradycardia and toxicity. 22. Tipranavir increases digoxin levels by inhibiting P-glycoprotein (P-gp) efflux transporters. Use caution and monitor closely, as there is a potential for increased toxicity. 23. Tobramycin increases digoxin levels by altering intestinal flora. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Use caution and monitor closely. 24. Tolvaptan increases digoxin levels by inhibiting P-glycoprotein (P-gp) efflux transporters. Both drugs can elevate serum potassium levels. Use caution and monitor closely. 25. Topiramate decreases digoxin levels through an unspecified interaction mechanism. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. Monitor closely. 26. Torsemide increases the effects of digoxin through pharmacodynamic synergy. Digoxin increases serum potassium, while torsemide decreases it. Use caution and monitor closely, as the interaction effect is unclear. 27. Trandolapril increases digoxin levels through an unspecified interaction mechanism. Use caution and monitor closely. 28. Trazodone decreases digoxin levels by inducing P-glycoprotein (P-gp) efflux transporters. Use caution and monitor closely. 29. Triamterene increases digoxin levels by competing for renal tubular clearance. Both drugs can elevate serum potassium levels. Modify therapy and monitor closely. 30. Trimethoprim increases digoxin levels by altering intestinal flora. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Use caution and monitor closely. 31. Trofinetide increases digoxin levels by inhibiting OATP1B1 and OATP1B3 transporters. Avoid or use an alternative drug, as this interaction may lead to increased plasma levels of OATP substrates. 32. Trosium chloride and digoxin both increase each other’s levels by reducing renal clearance. Use caution and monitor closely. 33. Tucatinib increases digoxin levels by inhibiting P-glycoprotein (P-gp) efflux transporters. Consider reducing the dosage of P-gp substrates, especially for drugs with a narrow therapeutic index, and monitor closely. 34. Ulipristal increases digoxin levels by inhibiting P-glycoprotein (P-gp) efflux transporters. Use caution and monitor closely. 35. Ustekinumab may alter CYP450 enzyme formation due to increased cytokine levels during chronic inflammation. Monitor therapeutic effects closely when initiating or discontinuing ustekinumab in patients receiving concomitant CYP450 substrates, particularly those with a narrow therapeutic index. 36. Valsartan increases digoxin levels by reducing renal clearance. Monitor digoxin levels closely when co-administered with drugs that may decrease glomerular filtration or tubular secretion. 37. Vancomycin increases digoxin levels by altering intestinal flora. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Use caution and monitor closely. 38. Vandetanib increases digoxin levels by inhibiting P-glycoprotein (P-gp) efflux transporters. Avoid or use an alternative drug. 39. Vemurafenib increases digoxin levels by inhibiting P-glycoprotein (P-gp) efflux transporters. Use caution and monitor closely. 40. Venetoclax increases digoxin levels by inhibiting P-glycoprotein (P-gp) efflux transporters. Avoid co-administration with narrow therapeutic index P-gp substrates. If unavoidable, administer the P-gp substrate at least 6 hours before venetoclax. 41. Verapamil increases digoxin levels by reducing renal clearance. Avoid or use an alternative drug, as this combination can increase the risk of toxicity. 42. Vincristine decreases digoxin levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Use caution and monitor closely. 43. Vitamin D may increase digoxin toxicity by causing hypercalcemia, which can lead to cardiac arrhythmias. Use caution and monitor closely. 44. Avoid rapid IV administration of digoxin in digitalized patients, as it may produce serious arrhythmias. Monitor for proarrhythmic effects, especially in cases of digoxin toxicity. 45. In patients with heart failure and preserved ventricular function, digoxin toxicity may occur more readily. Use caution and monitor closely. 46. Avoid switching between different oral forms or between brand and generic forms of digoxin, as bioavailability varies. Ensure proper monitoring of serum levels, as levels drawn within 6–8 hours of dosing may be falsely high due to prolonged distribution phases. 47. Consider digoxin use only in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction when symptoms persist despite guideline-directed medical therapy. Withdrawal of digoxin in clinically stable patients may lead to recurrence of heart failure symptoms. 48. In hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, avoid digoxin unless used to control ventricular response in atrial fibrillation. Digoxin may worsen outflow obstruction due to its positive inotropic effects. 49. Avoid extravasation during IV administration of digoxin. Ensure proper needle or catheter placement prior to and during administration. 50. Monitor serum concentrations closely when using digoxin for rate control in atrial fibrillation, as improper control of serum levels is associated with increased mortality risk.
